newsitem.title: USA: Blind cleric jailed in U.S. backs Egypt truce call.
newsitem.headline: Blind cleric jailed in U.S. backs Egypt truce call.

text.p: Sheikh Omar Abdel-Rahman, the blind cleric convicted in a plot to blow up New York City landmarks, has thrown his weight behind a recent call to his militant followers in Egypt to halt their violence against the government there, his lawyer said on Monday.

Abdel-Rahman issued a one-line statement from jail through his attorney, Ramsey Clark, who visited the fiery fundamentalist preacher last week at the Springfield Federal Facility in Missouri where he is serving a life sentence.

In July, six leaders of al-Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group) serving life sentences for their role in the 1981 assassination of President Anwar Sadat issued a statement in Egypt ordering followers to cease all military operations and refrain from inciting violence against the government.

"I give my blessing for the invitation to stop the violence and I ask others to support it," Abdel-Rahman told Clark to advise his followers. Clark told Reuters he had informed Abdel-Rahman via a translator of the truce call.

Abdel-Rahman, spiritual leader of Islamic Group, was convicted in 1995 for his role in a plot to blow up New York landmarks, including the United Nations, and to assassinate Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.
The appeal had been rejected by exiled Gama'a leaders, who said they would continue their armed struggle to transform Egypt into a strict Moslem state.
More than 1,000 people have been killed since the group took up arms in 1992 to overthrow the government and transform Egypt into a strict Islamic state.

Egyptian police say they have broken the back of the military wing of the Gama'a through crackdowns and the number of attacks has declined sharply since the mid-1990s, when the militants were killing about one policeman a day.
The Islamic Group is the main militant organisation in Egypt that has been at loggerheads with the Mubarak goverment.
Clark, a former U.S. attorney general, said the cleric was cut off from events in his homeland.

"The sheikh is in constant isolation. He is totally cut off from the outside world. No phone calls, no radio, no newspapers or magazines. He is not allowed to talk with anyone other than his lawyers and his wife, once a month in Egypt," Clark told Reuters.
The lawyer said he met with the cleric for about an hour in a room near his basement cell where Abdel-Rahman dictated the statement to him through a translator.

Clark said the sheikh, who he described as "frail and ailing," had lost about 10 pounds (4.5 kg) since his last visit with him a month ago. Abdel-Rahman suffers from diabetes and asthma and has a heart condition.
"He's not on a hunger strike but he is eating very little, just water and soup once a day," the lawyer said.
"The sheikh also told me he wasn't taking his medication because his conditions at the prison are much more harmful and threatening to his health than his diabetes and heart problems," Clark said.

Earlier on Monday, Egyptian Interior Minister Hassan el-Alfi welcomed the truce call reported in al-Hayat, saying: "Our main goal ... is to create a favourable atmosphere to attract investment and tourists. Therefore, we welcome any initiative that includes statements or actions which support this goal."
